items.title: Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs
items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have made remarkable progress on solving competition-level mathematics, yet their ability to verify natural-language mathematical proofs remains relatively underexplored. This gap is especially pronounced for Olympiad-level proofs, which require meticulous assessment of each claim in a long reasoning chain. Current proof verification thus primarily relies on expert inspection, which is costly to scale. In this paper, we present a systematic study of LLM-based verification in this setting. Specifically, we introduce a human-curated dataset of USAMO 2025 candidate solutions with expert grading, and conduct a broad evaluation of existing LLM verifiers across frontier models. We also propose TROJAN, an iterative self-critique pipeline for generating high-fidelity adversarial proofs at scale. Our comprehensive evaluation covers 20 models spanning seven metrics, two prompt styles, three inference methods, and three prompt templates, showing that state-of-the-art models still leave considerable room for improvement. To narrow this gap, we propose MABGrader, a Multi-Armed Bandit framework that reframes grading as arm selection over the discrete score space. MABGrader outperforms the SOTA ProofGrader by 26.4% in Quadratic Weighted Kappa and reduces grading error by 14%. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/aziksh-ospanov/TROJAN.

items.title: Evaluation-Guided Demonstration Refinement for Vision-Language-Action Policies: The Winning Entry in the MetaFine Open Competition
items.summary: We fine-tuned a separate $π_{0.5}$ policy for each of the five tasks in the MetaFine Open Competition, with a task-specific training mixture and number of actions executed per prediction. Training started from the official demonstrations and expert procedures. Local evaluation exposed recurring grasping, pushing, and insertion failures. We addressed them by revising the demonstrated motions and by adding expert continuations from states the policy reached, while keeping nominal demonstrations in training. Checkpoints were compared on every instruction, so that a gain on one instruction could not hide a loss on another. Our submission, MAI, ranked first overall with a score of 96.66.

items.title: Beyond the Evidence Coherence Trap: Agent-Driven Evidence Selection for Temporally Disordered Fake News Detection
items.summary: Fake news undermines public trust and the integrity of online information ecosystems. Temporally disordered fake news is especially elusive because it rearranges factual events into a false chronology. Individual events may remain factually valid even when their temporal relations are misrepresented. When similar events involving the same entity recur, retrieval may return semantically plausible evidence from the wrong period. Consequently, independent event verification may rely on locally coherent but temporally mismatched evidence and incorrectly validate the article. We call this the \textit{evidence coherence trap}. Because existing benchmarks rarely isolate this setting, we construct ChronoFake, a source-disjoint benchmark of 30,706 articles derived from temporally anchored real events. It distinguishes temporal manipulation from valid narration, including flashbacks. To address this, we propose DelSA, a \underline{D}ocument S\underline{el}ection \underline{S}elf-Updating \underline{A}gent that iteratively refines evidence selection during training and applies a frozen rulebook for one-pass evidence selection at inference. DelSA uses an LLM to characterize candidate evidence, while a verifier-trained reranker balances local relevance against timeline consistency. Finally, the classifier compares the article-implied chronology extracted by the LLM with the evidence-derived chronology to reveal global temporal conflicts. items.title: The Vocabulary Is Already Here: Adapting Pretrained Interpretable Features for Generative Recommendation
items.summary: Generative recommendation (GR) predicts the next item through its semantic ID (SID). Existing methods commonly fit SID vocabularies to pretrained language model (PLM) representations of item descriptions, incurring additional training costs and making vocabulary coverage dependent on the fitting domains. We observe that pretrained sparse autoencoders expose PLM features with human-interpretable semantic annotations, allowing feature indices to serve as a reusable SID vocabulary. However, reusing this vocabulary requires preserving item distinctions under compact token budgets and learning to favor target items over candidates with shared dominant features. It also requires extending feature interpretability from item content to retrieval decisions. To address these challenges, we propose API, a framework that Adapts the Pretrained Interpretable vocabulary for effective and explainable GR without additional vocabulary learning. Within API, Pretrained Interpretable IDs (PIDs) retain selected feature indices and relative activation strengths for item discrimination. With PIDs as supervision, the Semantic Prediction Adapter (SPA) learns user preferences from interaction histories through joint feature-index and strength prediction. SPA combines both predictions to score candidate items, with item-level supervision encouraging the observed next item to outrank its alternatives. API further explains candidate score differences through feature contributions paired with their pretrained semantic annotations. Extensive experiments show that API achieves competitive performance across backbones and decoding schemes, while preserving item distinctions under compact token budgets and enabling explainable retrieval.

items.title: Making Self-Driving Laboratories Auditable:A Unified Framework for Hybrid Actions,Measurements, and Safe Execution
items.summary: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) are laboratory systems that couple experimental planning, automated execution, and measurement feedback in a closed loop. Integrating flexible robot control with the typed application programming interfaces (APIs) and continuous measurements exposed by laboratory instruments remains an execution-interface challenge. To address this challenge, we propose a traceable framework comprising four components: LAM (Lab Action Model), OpenSDL, Safe-SDL, and L3-Bench. LAM is a proposed measurement-conditioned policy architecture that extends vision-language-action paradigms to generate both continuous robot trajectories and typed instrument API calls. OpenSDL is an execution substrate with an initial control implementation, designed to map role-level operations to heterogeneous devices, coordinate execution, and record timestamped causal events. The proposed Safe-SDL runtime gate combines pre-dispatch schema and resource checks with signal temporal logic monitoring during execution, including extended waiting periods. L3-Bench (Level-3 Laboratory Benchmark) specifies an episode-level evaluation protocol covering physical outcomes, timing, reproducibility, safety violations, and fault recovery. Together, these components provide an end-to-end design for linking hybrid action generation, monitored device execution, measurement feedback, and experimental evaluation, addressing coordination and traceability challenges in SDL workflows.

items.title: GeoGSplat: Geometry-Grounded Non-Pixel-Aligned Gaussian Splatting
items.summary: Feed-forward Gaussian Splatting enables efficient novel view synthesis, but pixel-aligned prediction makes the primitive count grow with image resolution and view count, leading to substantial redundancy and increased computational cost. Non-pixel-aligned methods address this limitation by predicting a fixed number of Gaussians. Without explicit ray and depth constraints, these methods yield misplaced Gaussian centers, causing rendering artifacts under large viewpoint changes. To address this issue, we introduce GeoGSplat, a geometry-grounded feed-forward model that explicitly incorporates geometric priors into the non-pixel-aligned framework. A dual-branch encoder constructs Anchors and Triplane to capture coarse 3D structure and fine-grained scene features, respectively. Subsequently, a hierarchical decoder progressively decodes dense 3D points and Gaussian primitives, enabling 3D reconstruction and novel view synthesis. GeoGSplat surpasses both state-of-the-art pixel-aligned and non-pixel-aligned Gaussian Splatting methods on DTU and NRGBD in terms of novel view synthesis and reconstruction. The advantage of our geometry-grounded paradigm further increases as target viewpoints move farther from the input cameras, demonstrating stronger generalization to large viewpoint changes. items.title: DocSkill: Skill-Integrated Agentic Reasoning for Multilingual Multi-Hop Document Question Answering
items.summary: Multilingual multi-hop document question answering (MMHop-DocQA) requires locating and integrating evidence across complex layouts, document pages, and diverse languages. Existing approaches include single-pass processing and adaptive tool use, but learning to coordinate evidence acquisition, cross-page integration, and answer verification remains challenging. To address this challenge, we present DocSkill, an agentic framework with a learned skill-orchestration policy for adaptive evidence acquisition and reasoning. The policy selects, revisits, or skips skills according to the evolving evidence state. To construct supervision for skill orchestration, bounded Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) explores alternative skill trajectories offline. These trajectories provide demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and preference pairs for Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). We further introduce MMHop-DocBench, a multilingual multi-hop document QA dataset with training and test splits, containing 60K QA pairs across 10 languages and eight document domains. Its HopGen pipeline builds hierarchical page-element graphs to derive traceable cross-page evidence paths and generate grounded QA pairs with page- and element-level evidence annotations. Experiments show that DocSkill with Qwen3-VL-8B achieves 41.0 accuracy and 49.2 F1 on MMHop-DocBench, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline by 5.5 and 6.3 points, respectively, and achieving competitive performance on MMLongBench-Doc and DocBench.

items.title: TCSP3.0: Template-Based Crystal Structure Prediction with Coefficient-Preserving Element Substitution and Structural Diversity
items.summary: Template-based crystal structure prediction (CSP) transfers a known crystal structure to a new composition by element substitution, so its accuracy depends on retrieving suitable templates, mapping elements and ranking the resulting candidates correctly. Auditing the original TCSP2.0 implementation on the T180 benchmark, we found that 469 of its 2,347 selected structures (20%) have the wrong composition, caused by element mappings that ignore stoichiometric coefficients and by sequential text substitution that cascades or corrupts element symbols. We propose TCSP3.0, which enforces coefficient-preserving mappings, substitutes species simultaneously on parsed structures and validates every candidate's composition and cell. It further adds periodic-number retrieval, soft oxidation-state evidence, radius-compatibility scoring, structural deduplication, and ORB-v3 machine-learning-potential relaxation and energy ranking of its candidates, as used by deep generative CSP baselines. TCSP3.0 achieves Top-1 and Top-20 match rates of 72.2% and 90.6% on T180, compared with 28.3% and 45.6% for TCSP2.0, and a Top-20 match rate of 74.0% on a new 800-target benchmark (T800). On T180 it also outperforms PNcsp+ and deep generative models CrystalFlow and MaskGXT (Top-1 72.2% versus at most 63.9%). Even without relaxation, TCSP3.0 reaches 67.8% at Top-1 and 90.6% at Top-20 in a median of 28 s per target on two CPU cores, about ten times faster than CrystalFlow. Paired ten-arm ablations on T180 and T800 show that most of the improvement comes from the correctness fixes; structural deduplication significantly improves the Top-5 match rate, embedding-based retrieval is required for coverage, and the remaining scoring features have small or null effects.

items.title: Explaining Navigation Decisions: Stage-Aware Visual Attribution for Vision-Language Navigation
items.summary: As Vision-Language Models (VLMs) increasingly enable robots to follow language instructions, understanding their navigation decisions becomes important for reliable deployment. Existing explainability methods overlook a key challenge in Vision-Language Navigation (VLN): evidence for the current action may be distributed across historical and current observations and associated with different instruction stages. We identify instruction-stage insensitivity, where existing methods produce similar explanations despite changes across different navigation stages. To address this issue, we propose a stage-aware attribution framework for VLN. We first construct action-conditioned temporal instruction--visual attributions across observations. These attributions are projected into instruction space to estimate stage associations, which guide the aggregation of relevant historical evidence for refining the current explanation. An instruction-guided spatial filter further suppresses isolated responses while preserving compact, instruction-relevant regions. Experiments across multiple VLN policies and benchmarks show improved attribution quality over existing methods. We further demonstrate that our method acts as a diagnostic tool for analyzing failure cases, and validate its applicability to real-world navigation on a Unitree G1 robot.

items.title: When Does GEPA Merge Help? A Mechanism-Level Diagnostic
items.summary: GEPA is among the strongest reflective prompt optimizers for language-model programs, but its system-aware merge operator is unstable across models: merge improves gpt-4.1-mini on average while degrading Qwen3-8B, an asymmetry noted but left unexplained by the GEPA paper. We investigate this instability across five datasets and two models. Our nine-configuration sweep over merge timing and merge operator shows that merge can improve both models when configured appropriately. This suggests that merge instability is better explained by configuration sensitivity than by an inherent flaw in the merge operator. We then test whether prompt-level features predict GEPA's merge-accept decisions and find that they do not, ruling out static-feature gating. As a proof of concept, a behavior-based probe built from these diagnostics avoids large merge failures in our multi-seed runs by abstaining on high-risk tasks, although it does not consistently outperform NoMerge. Code is available as GEPA-MergeProbe at https://github.com/ChongZZZZ/GEPA_MERGE .

items.title: The Symmetry of Differential Neural Tangent Kernel under the Orthogonal Group
items.summary: The differential neural tangent kernel (DNTK) is a tool for analyzing the training dynamics of overparameterized physics informed neural networks. In this work, we investigate the symmetry of the infinite DNTK under an orthogonal group, for two layer and deep neural networks separately, based on the explicit expression of the DNTK and recursive formula, respectively. The results are for all activations with or without a bias term, and shed insight into the structure of the infinite width DNTK. Then we prove that the integral operators over the unit sphere induced by operators from the same group orbit share the spectrum, and their reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces differ only by an orthogonal transformation, and that the operator fixed DNTK exhibits zonal symmetry on the unit sphere for symmetric operators. Thus the eigenvalue decay rate of the associated integral operator can be derived for shallow networks with RePU activation and zero bias initialization.

items.title: Deep Scientific Reasoning under Physical Constraints: Structure-Aware Spectrum Prediction
items.summary: Structured scientific spectra encode rich physical information while obeying hard constraints, such as conservation laws and characteristic spectral geometry. Accurate prediction of these spectra is central to materials discovery, yet existing methods often treat them as unconstrained sequences and therefore fail to enforce the underlying physical structure. Taking electronic density of states (eDOS) as the prototypical example, we introduce DeepSciReasoner, a general paradigm for predicting scientific spectra under physical constraints. The framework combines structure-aware spectrum decoding with constraint-preserving physical reasoning, allowing predictions to capture rich spectral structure while respecting the underlying physics. We evaluate DeepSciReasoner on eDOS, phonon density of states (phDOS), X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES), and Raman spectra, where it substantially improves prediction accuracy while maintaining physical consistency. These results establish DeepSciReasoner as a reusable blueprint for structured scientific spectrum prediction under hard physical constraints.

items.title: BriLLM-MetaPred: A Representation-Prediction Unity Language Model with Adaptive Self-Measurement
items.summary: We present BriLLM-MetaPred, the first engineering implementation of the MetaPred machine-learning framework established by a mathematical theory of AGI, instantiated for language modeling. The theory argues that MetaPred is both necessary and sufficient as a machine-learning primitive for general cognition. Taking this theoretical conclusion as a design premise, we report an implementation of the primitive for language modeling. A single continuously evolving dynamical state serves as both the context representation and the state from which predictions are read out. Continuous measurement of its own state reduces finite-depth inconsistency, maintains internal consistency, and provides an endogenous dynamical self-supervision signal in fixed-point form. The single dynamical state of MetaPred intrinsically couples training and inference. MetaPred therefore exhibits symmetry across almost all key elements of machine learning, an intuitive and observable property of the mathematical optimum over the space of all machine-learning paradigms. BriLLM-MetaPred is neither another recurrent language model nor an extension of BriLLM. It provides a bridge between two prior contributions: the construction and motivation of the MetaPred primitive provided by AGI theory, and the SiFu learning paradigm provided by BriLLM (Zhao et al., 2025). The latter's node-signal-flow design enables the primitive to run on available software and hardware accelerators. Our implementation of BriLLM-MetaPred achieves predictive performance comparable to a GPT baseline of the same size. This provides initial evidence for the engineering feasibility of the MetaPred framework established by the mathematical theory of AGI. MetaPred is the first machine-learning paradigm derived entirely from mathematical theory rather than assembled and incrementally improved through human design---and perhaps the last such paradigm.

items.title: The Information Geometry of Representation Formation
items.summary: Most analyses of neural representations focus on trained endpoints, leaving the process by which internal structure forms comparatively unmeasured. We instead treat representation formation itself as an object of study, asking whether the path a representation takes through training reveals information that its endpoint does not. We formalize this idea by viewing representation learning as a geometric trajectory, using Bures geometry to measure movement through representation space and quantum Fisher information to characterize local sensitivity to input factors. We find that learning concentrates local sensitivity on task-relevant factors, and that changing only the prediction target reorganizes this geometry around the corresponding visual factor. More strikingly, representation trajectories become systematically less direct as the learned computation requires higher-order interactions among input factors. This effect persists under matched-performance and training-duration controls and transfers from synthetic vector inputs to residual CNNs on rendered and natural images. Importantly, formation history contains predictive information about the stability of the learned representation: controlling for interaction order, path tortuosity predicts its subsequent drift under continued training and sensitivity to parameter perturbations, whereas endpoint displacement does not. Finally, representation-aware optimization lets us actively shape these trajectories, showing that formation geometry is not only measurable but actionable. Together, these results establish representation formation as a new source of information about learning: its geometry reveals properties of the computation being constructed, predicts subsequent representational stability, and provides a target for intervention during optimization.

items.title: The Patient Is Always Right? Evaluating Sycophancy in Medical Diagnosis with Graded Patient Beliefs
items.summary: More people are seeking out general-purpose AI models for medical advice, including diagnosis. Yet, AI models are susceptible to sycophancy, like validating users' beliefs even when they are untrue, which could lead to false positive diagnoses. Here, we evaluate how nine AI models change their diagnostic decision when a patient presents a belief that they have a specific (but incorrect) medical condition. We vary how close the user belief is to the clinical evidence presented. Models sycophantically adopt the patient's belief on average 23.2\% of the time---sometimes even when the patient proposes a fictional, made-up condition. We also varied different personas, including a Rare Disease Claimer that got models to accept their belief 43.0\% of the time. Additional analyses find that medical fine-tuning and model scale makes models less susceptible to changing their diagnoses. Sycophantic bias in medical diagnosis raises implications for safety, especially as more people are using AI for health support.

items.title: Reversible Pseudonymisation of Documents Sent to External LLMs: an Open Bilingual Benchmark and an Engine
items.summary: Professionals send working documents to external large language models. A common safeguard is reversible pseudonymisation: personal data are replaced with placeholders before the request and restored locally in the answer. We present an open benchmark of five existing open tools and a regular-expression baseline on Russian and UK English, and an open engine built on the two strongest tools. The benchmark excludes each tool's own authors' dataset from its verdict, compares the engine with each tool on identical datasets for detection, reports masking precision, and tests on a held-out set of synthetic documents whose files, hashes, decision rules, run plan and stopping rule were published before any run. Two local LLMs test whether placeholders survive. All evaluation data are synthetic, and the benchmark was run by the author of the engine; code, data, predictions and raw answers are released. On external datasets no existing tool meets all predefined thresholds: in UK English the identifier and leak thresholds are not met, in Russian the identifier threshold is borderline. On the last held-out set of 1,000 documents per language, the best existing tools leave a whole value visible in 61% (Russian) and 58% (UK) of documents. On these documents, from the generator it was developed on, the engine does so in 0.3% [0.1; 0.9] and 0.2% [0.1; 0.7], leaves any part of a value visible in 0.8% and 0.2%, and meets all detection thresholds in both languages. In UK English it also restores at least 99% of its placeholders after 760 answers. In Russian it restores only 94.6% [93.6; 95.6] of name placeholders, against a 99% threshold, mainly because the inflection it borrows from pii-guard produces wrong surname forms. The engine was developed over six earlier held-out sets from the same generator; real documents were not tested.

items.title: Cross-User Adaptation for sEMG Gesture Recognition via Continual Learning
items.summary: Prosthetic and assistive interfaces increasingly depend on decoding hand gestures from surface electromyography (sEMG). Because the signal is shaped by person-specific factors, the recurrent neural networks (RNNs) commonly used to model these temporal streams must adapt to new wearers and new gesture classes after deployment. Continual learning (CL) enables this adaptation without retraining from scratch, yet applying it to recurrent sEMG models is not straightforward. Standard recurrent training practices can destabilize learning, and which CL strategy holds up under realistic cross-user drift is unestablished. We evaluate three representative CL strategies under domain- and class-incremental drift on NinaPro DB1, and find experience replay to outperform elastic weight consolidation (EWC) and naive fine-tuning. It reaches 83.3% final accuracy for class-incremental drift while limiting forgetting to 1.8-5.8% accuracy drop, as against 16.2-28.5% for EWC and naive training. We further show these models must be trained on shuffled, independently-windowed segments. Streaming windows in temporal order collapses the network into predicting a single dominant gesture, while a shuffled, stateless regime trains stably. Finally, hand-crafted time-domain features raise per-task accuracy by up to about 40% over raw signals, but only replay preserves that gain under class-incremental drift.

items.title: Fed-Universe: A Semantic-Geometric-Topological-Human (S-G-T-H) Stack for Negotiated Alignment in Federated Systems
items.summary: Conventional federated learners implicitly optimize for global means, creating a "one-size-fits-all" paradigm that inevitably suppresses the minority under cross-site heterogeneity. To bridge this critical gap, we present Fed-Universe, a generalizable Semantic-Geometric-Topological-Human (S-G-T-H) architecture that transforms passive averaging into an active negotiation for decentralized alignment. The S-layer deploys an edge-capable LLM as a semantic surrogate to translate heterogeneous inputs into standardized patient profile prompts. The G-layer enforces geometric quality assurance (GQA) via a mapping f: Theta -> Q from the statistical parameter space to a physically interpretable quality domain, employing a cosine similarity gate to retain minority updates based on physical geometry rather than statistical proximity. The T-layer executes topological Pareto control, identifying a sensitivity-based knee point (lambda_k) to balance multi-objective aggregation without majority degradation. Finally, the H-layer operationalizes a cognitive twin dynamic to mirror the user's real-time psychological state, dynamically adapting human-computer interaction modes via active intent alignment. To ground this theoretical architecture empirically, we validated the S-G-T core on a binational synthetic clinical network simulation. This proof-of-concept demonstrated a "zero-sum escape": a minority node (<3% data volume) achieved utility parity (loss reduction from 0.857 to 0.340) alongside dominant hubs. Our Fed-Universe framework is being expanded along two focused pillars: institutional multimodal alignment (Fed-Ultra) and individual cognitive intent alignment (Fed-Human).

items.title: Partial Modal Tensor Regression
items.summary: With the rapid development of modern scientific research, tensor data have become increasingly prevalent across a wide range of fields. How to effectively characterize the relationship between tensor predictors and a response while preserving the intrinsic structure of tensor data has therefore become an important problem in high-dimensional statistical analysis. Existing tensor regression methods mainly focus on conditional means or conditional quantiles. When the response distribution is asymmetric, heavy-tailed, or contaminated by outlying observations, the conditional modal provides a robust and interpretable alternative characterization. In this paper, we propose a partial modal tensor regression (PMTR) method. The proposed method constructs the partial modal tensor covariance, which incorporates information on the conditional modal to guide tensor dimension reduction, and subsequently establishes a modal tensor regression model in the reduced tensor space. This strategy alleviates the dimensionality burden caused by direct vectorization while preserving the intrinsic structural information of tensor predictors. Under suitable regularity conditions, we establish the consistency and asymptotic properties of the proposed estimators and employ a data-driven dimension-selection procedure to determine the effective dimension along each tensor mode.

items.title: Steering the Teacher: Improving On-Policy Self-Distillation for Thinking Models
items.summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) trains a student on its own reasoning trajectories using token-level supervision from a reference-conditioned teacher initialized from the same model. However, access to the reference can induce teacher behaviors that undermine independent reasoning in thinking models, leading to reference hallucinations, where the student cites an unavailable reference to justify reasoning steps, and reconsideration suppression, where the teacher discourages verification and revision at uncertain steps. We introduce Steered-Teacher OPSD (ST-OPSD) to jointly address these failure modes through activation steering. ST-OPSD extracts two directions from model-generated reasoning trajectories and applies them to the teacher's hidden states during distillation target computation, suppressing reference-invoking behavior and encouraging reconsideration with marker-family calibration. The student learns from the resulting teacher distributions without being steered. Experiments on AIME and HMMT show that ST-OPSD improves accuracy over vanilla OPSD and other interventions while restoring reconsideration and reference-hallucination rates to base-model levels.

items.title: Resolving the Mobility-Equity-Emissions Trilemma: A Causal Machine Learning Framework for Dynamic Tolling Policy
items.summary: We propose a causal machine learning framework to integrate dynamic tolling for mobility, equity, and climate objectives, resolving a long-standing policy trilemma. Using Double Machine Learning, we estimate zone-type-specific treatment effects, showing that commercial zones yield nearly twice the delay reduction of residential zones. Our adaptive quota mechanism expands residential coverage 34-fold while preserving 93% of total delay savings and sustaining high return on investment. The framework delivers climate co-benefits, reducing emissions by 743.5 metric tons of CO2 (valued at 141 USD) via congestion-sensitive pricing under moderate traffic conditions with sensitivity bounds from 557.6 to 929.3 tons. Crucially, we uncover a policy-invariant toll range where performance remains robust across demand scenarios, simplifying implementation. This study reveals critical, previously unidentified insights, such as a policy-invariant toll range, that can significantly simplify real-world implementation. Validated on synthetic data mirroring real-world networks, our methodological advances lay the foundation for future public deployment.

items.title: Hybrid Mamba-Transformer Network for Single-Shot 3D Reconstruction from Fringe Patterns
items.summary: Deep learning facilitates rapid single shot three dimensional (3D) reconstruction using fringe projection profilometry (FPP), but recovering accurate surface height from a single high frequency fringe image remains challenging because both long-range spatial consistency and fine geometric details must be preserved. Convolutional networks are limited in modeling long range dependencies, whereas window-based Transformers establish global interactions only progressively with increasing depth. To address these limitations, a hybrid Mamba Transformer network is proposed for fringe to height regression. The network adopts a Swin based U shaped architecture and introduces visual state space modeling at the intermediate resolution encoder stage. An axial and dilated vision state space (ADVSS) block is further developed to enhance prescan feature encoding through local, dilated, and axial depthwise convolutions while retaining four directional selective scanning. This design combines linear complexity long range modeling with direction aware preservation of local fringe structures. Experiments on a publicly available FPP dataset show that the proposed method outperforms hNet, SwinConvUNet, UHRNet, and HiDNet in mean absolute error(MAE), root mean square error (RMSE), absolute relative error, and structural similarity index measure (SSIM). Using only one deformed fringe image, the proposed method achieves an RMSE of 0.548 mm and an SSIM of 0.9985, reducing RMSE by 65.2% and 59.6% relative to UHRNet and HiDNet, respectively. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining selective state space modeling with hierarchical window based attention for accurate single-shot FPP reconstruction.

items.title: Constrained Gradient Equilibrium: Approachability under Locally Constrained Adversaries
items.summary: Gradient equilibrium (GEQ) is a recent framework in online learning that requires the time-averaged gradients along the learner's trajectory to vanish. We study GEQ when the learner is constrained and ask when such an equilibrium remains achievable in an adversarial environment. We first show that constrained GEQ (CGEQ) can be impossible even under simple and slowly varying constraints, motivating imposing local temporal structure on the adversary. We then develop an approachability framework for CGEQ under locally constrained adversaries, and obtain necessary and sufficient characterizations in the spirit of classical Blackwell approachability. Beyond these theoretical characterizations, we provide an algorithmic principle that converts window-wise no-regret learners into CGEQ algorithms under a local feasibility condition with margin. Experiments on synthetic and real data demonstrate that the resulting algorithms perform strongly in both achieving GEQ and respecting the constraints.

items.title: EmoNet: A Lightweight Attention-Based CNN for Speech Emotion Recognition
items.summary: Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) is a fundamental task in affective computing that enables applications such as mental health assessment, human-computer interaction, and automated customer support systems. Accurate emotion classification from speech remains challenging due to variations in speaker style, acoustic conditions, and the high computational cost of modern deep learning approaches. Many existing systems depend on large transformer-based architectures that require substantial computational resources, making them less suitable for real-time or resource-constrained environments. This research proposes EmoNet, a lightweight deep learning framework for speech emotion classification across seven emotion categories. The model is built on a four-block depthwise separable CNN encoder with squeeze-and-excitation attention and residual connections, combined with a Bidirectional LSTM for temporal feature learning and a multi-head attention pooling mechanism for improved representation. A comprehensive 134-channel acoustic feature set alongside data augmentation techniques including audio-level perturbations and SpecAugment is employed to improve robustness under diverse acoustic conditions. Evaluated on a combined dataset of TESS, RAVDESS, and SAVEE, EmoNet achieves a test accuracy of 96.75% with only 4.11 million parameters. The proposed model outperforms its reproduced baseline and remains competitive with significantly larger state-of-the-art architectures.

items.title: "High-Quality" Data for Early-Stage Instruction Tuning: An Empirical Study of Data Quality Metrics
items.summary: "Data quality" is widely invoked in instruction tuning, but the term is often underspecified. We study it as an operational property by asking which simple example-level metrics, drawn from prior work on data selection, text quality, and instruction tuning, best predict training utility under a fixed finetuning budget. For each metric, we sort instruction-response examples by score, partition them into low, middle, and high bins with roughly equal token mass, finetune separately on each bin, and compare validation perplexity and LLM-as-judge scores for the models' generated answers as a function of cumulative training tokens. Our results suggest that answer-dense supervision, as captured by response ratio, is a stronger and more portable predictor of instruction-tuning utility than commonly used alternative proxies.

items.title: Hierarchical Cooperative GFlowNets
items.summary: Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) are trained to sample objects from compositional spaces with probability proportional to a reward function, but ineffective exploration can cause learned samplers to concentrate on a few high-reward regions. An intuitive remedy is to train multiple GFlowNets independently in parallel and combine their samples. However, this does not prevent multiple models from collapsing onto the same high-reward areas, leaving large regions of the state space unexplored. With this in mind, we propose Hierarchical Cooperative GFlowNets (HCG), an approach that dynamically partitions the search space to coordinate discovery without relying on hand-crafted boundaries. HCG imposes an ordering in which the highest-ranked model may explore the entire space, while lower-ranked models are progressively pushed toward regions not covered by higher-ranked ones. We provide a theoretical characterization of how specific learning objectives can shift probability mass away from designated areas, instantiating this mechanism within our architecture. A shared classifier coordinates the hierarchy by partitioning the search space, keeping the GFlowNets independently parameterized and enabling asynchronous training. Furthermore, we derive a normalizer-weighted aggregation rule for the ensemble and prove that it recovers the target reward-proportional distribution under the stated assumptions. Finally, experiments across multimodal distributions, sequence generation, combinatorial optimization, and biological sequence design show that HCG improves mode coverage and target approximation, translating increases in the number of coordinated samplers into broader, complementary exploration.

items.title: Performance of Neural Operator Baselines on 'The Well' Dataset
items.summary: The Well, a 15-terabyte dataset spanning 16 physical simulation domains, provides an extensive benchmark for developing and evaluating machine learning surrogate models for complex physical systems. The baselines released with the benchmark were presented by their authors as illustrative examples obtained at small computational cost, trained with zero to very limited hyperparameter tuning and under a highly constraining 12-hour per-run wall-clock limit. These results have subsequently been treated as fully tuned benchmarks, and in some cases effectively interpreted as unconstrained performance baselines. We perform a short non-exhaustive hyperparameter search for the Tucker-factorized Fourier Neural Operator (TFNO) under the same 12-hour per-run wall-clock limit, while using only a single input timestep rather than the history of up to four used by the published baselines. Despite this more restrictive setup, tuning alone reduces VRMSE below both published FNO and TFNO baselines on 15 of 17 tasks, sometimes by several orders of magnitude. This sensitivity to a modest tuning effort underscores that the released neural operator baselines should not be treated as architectural benchmarks.

items.title: InteractiveWorld: A Verifiable Human-Centric Environment for Building Better Interactive MLLM Assistants
items.summary: People have long dreamed of an assistant that is always there to guide them and remind what they forget, from new dishes to lost keys. Powered by multimodal large language models (MLLMs), egocentric AI assistants on wearable devices are bringing this dream within reach: they see what the user sees and give instructions for user's physical work when necessary. However, testing such assistance is challenging and usually requires real people. The expensive and rare real interaction data leaves a key question unanswered: Can today's MLLMs truly help people in physical world? To answer this question, we propose InteractiveWorld, the first verifiable environment for closed-loop interaction between human and AI assistant. Unlike existing robot-centric simulators, InteractiveWorld lets the assistant guide a human agent who observes the scene, understands instructions, and acts independently. It thus realistically simulates how AI assistant collaborates with human: the assistant instructs, the human acts, and the environment executes actions and updates what they see next. Building on it, we introduce InteractiveBench, the first dynamic benchmark for egocentric AI assistants, with 120 multi-turn tasks across six categories. In each task, the assistant guides the human in real time, and every instruction shapes the outcome, which is scored by verifiable, state-based rewards. Experiments with 12 frontier MLLMs show they are still far from reliable assistants. Even the strongest model, Claude Fable 5.1, achieves at most 20% and 25% on long-horizon Guidance and Planning tasks, respectively. Overall, our work offers a verifiable platform and a rigorous evaluation set, laying a solid foundation for research on interactive MLLM assistants that truly help people in the physical world.

items.title: Accuracy Is Not Enough: An Efficiency- and Statistics-Aware Benchmark of ResNet50 and Vision Transformer for Explainable Multi-Class Gastrointestinal Diseases Classification
items.summary: Automated classification of gastrointestinal (GI) findings in endoscopic images could support early diagnosis, but architectures are often chosen on accuracy alone. We present a controlled, reproducible benchmark of ResNet50 and ViT-B/16 for eight-class GI classification on the public Kvasir dataset (4,000 images), using a stratified split (400 test images) and stratified group 5-fold cross-validation over all images. In cross-validation, ResNet50 and ViT-B/16 reached 92.12% and 91.70% accuracy, and a two one-sided tests (TOST) procedure showed equivalence within a +/-3 percentage-point margin (difference +0.43 points, 90% CI -0.33 to +1.18; p < 0.001). The architectures differed mainly in cost: ResNet50 had 3.6 times fewer parameters and 4.3 times fewer operations, 2.5-fold lower single-image CPU latency (69 vs. 177 ms) and 3.8-fold higher GPU throughput. Cross-validated calibration was similar (expected calibration error 0.021 vs. 0.023). An edge-oriented transformer, MobileViT-S, was most accurate on the test split (95.5%) but lost 9.4 points when an acquisition artefact present in some classes (the ScopeGuide inset) was occluded, whereas ResNet50 was not significantly affected. On 500 unseen polyp images with expert masks, both models' Grad-CAM maps focused on the lesion (3.6 times chance). On a de-duplicated external subset of GastroVision (1,998 images), accuracy fell to 78-80% for all three models and differences between them remained small. Accuracy differences between architectures were thus small relative to the effects of shortcut learning and domain shift, whereas efficiency differences were large. An efficient CNN is a defensible default for resource-constrained screening, but no model is deployment-ready without local validation.

items.title: QECGBERT: A Scalable ECG Foundation Model Based on Self-Supervised Language Learning via VQ-VAE Waveform Tokenization
items.summary: AI foundation models play a pivotal role in advancing heart disease diagnosis from electrocardiogram (ECG) data, particularly for rare diseases where the lack of sufficient labeled data hinders supervised learning. However, most self-supervised learning methods treat ECGs as generic sequence or image data without exploiting underlying physiological structure. To address this limitation, we propose QECGBERT, a self-supervised ECG language model that explicitly encodes physiological semantics by tokenizing the P, QRS, T, and isoelectric background waveforms. Vector-quantized variational autoencoder (VQ-VAE) tokenization is applied to each 12-lead ECG, with tokens enriched by continuous waveform features to preserve morphology lost during quantization without increasing sequence length. This design enables compact BERT masked language modeling with short sequences, improving scalability and reducing computational cost relative to long-sequence approaches. QECGBERT applies BERT pre-training to the MIMIC-IV dataset containing over 800,000 unlabeled ECG recordings, and fine-tuning on labeled PTB-XL, CPSC2018, and Chapman--Shaoxing--Ningbo datasets for evaluation. The results demonstrate that QECGBERT achieves comparable or superior performance to published benchmarks, offering a scalable, physiologically aware approach to ECG foundation modeling for cardiac diagnosis.

items.title: Beyond Belief: Evaluating and Mitigating LLM Susceptibility to Misinformation
items.summary: Tool-using large language models (LLMs) must decide whether external information warrants action. We investigate whether their expressed credibility judgments reliably indicate behavioral resistance to misinformation. We evaluate five LLMs on 196 constructed false notices paired with legitimate counterparts and 204 archived attacks adapted to simulated tool use. When asked to act on the constructed notices, models issue harmful tool calls in 27%--99% of cases they have rated untrustworthy. Removing the preliminary rating step increases harmful execution by 15 percentage points on average, showing that credibility elicitation itself changes the behavior being evaluated. Interventions that improve credibility discrimination do not consistently yield safer actions. A simple forewarning significantly reduces harmful execution in four of five models, but neither tested generated-example prebunk outperforms it in the main evaluation. These reductions can also compromise legitimate task completion. Supervised fine-tuning on generated false notices reduces harmful execution on held-out archived attacks under the rating-first protocol, with model-dependent utility costs and weaker protection without rating elicitation. Our findings motivate evaluating misinformation defenses through both harmful actions and legitimate task completion, while accounting for the behavioral effects of the evaluation protocol.

items.title: I Won't Know Until I Try: Interactive Information Gathering for Long-Horizon Manipulation
items.summary: Long-horizon manipulation often depends on object properties that cannot be reliably inferred from appearance alone. Physical interaction can reveal these properties, but it can also change the world in ways that invalidate subsequent actions. We present a task and motion planning (TAMP) framework that integrates task-directed interactive information-gathering with interleaved planning and execution. Building on PDDLStream, our framework plans optimistically with these interactive actions, verifies their outcomes during execution, and adapts the remaining plan by retaining still-applicable actions and replanning only the connections needed to continue execution. We evaluate the framework in simulation and on a real robot across tasks that require determining whether an object is movable, a pen has ink, a drawer can be opened, or a container is empty. These experiments demonstrate how interaction-driven state updates and recovery replanning support continued execution under uncertain outcomes and external disturbances.

items.title: How Do Small Coding Agents Use Code Graphs and Embeddings?
items.summary: Coding agents are given embedding search and code-graph tools on the premise that a repository's structure is something the model lacks and the tool supplies. We test that premise on SWE-bench Verified with small open-weight models, stratifying tasks by a deterministic hop depth (the shortest code-graph path from code the issue mentions to code the gold patch changes) that a companion paper defines and validates. First, we ablate a localization agent's tool set (grep only; +embedding search; +graph tools; all) on a depth-balanced 160-task split and on all 500 tasks for ten models (six Qwen3 sizes from 0.6B to 32B with five decodings each, an FP8 control, three Gemma 4 sizes; 79k episodes). Structured tools double grep-only accuracy for Qwen3-8B and Gemma 4 E4B; their gain peaks at 17-21 points at 1.7-4B and falls to 4-5 points at 32B (odds ratio 0.77-0.82 per doubling of parameters). From 8B up, about half of that gain is the form of the submission rather than finding the target; the fall from 14B to 32B is a fall in tool uptake at equal grep-only accuracy; and the same 4B size gains or does not gain from a tool depending on the checkpoint. Each extra hop multiplies the odds of correct localization by 0.50-0.67 at every size, and no tool set flattens that gradient: traces show the graph tools' gain is name lookup at hop 0 and one expansion at hop 1, and agents chain expansions in only 12-14% of episodes. A fixed repair model resolves 6-13 of 160 tasks from these localizations (oracle 26). Second, linear probes find direct call edges decodable under a within-anchor, degree-stratified protocol (AUC 0.74; 0.61-0.66 inside agent conversations), but below a lexical baseline (0.99), with two-hop edges at 0.57. Small agents carry a one-hop, largely lexical picture of their repository, in weights and in use. We release the agent, probes, logs and traces.

items.title: A Nonconvex Framework for Joint Sparse Sample Weighting and Parameter Estimation
items.summary: We propose a joint sparse sample weighting and parameter estimation (SWAPE) framework that jointly optimizes model parameters and sample weights to train a model while simultaneously assigning an individual weight to each training data point. Our framework accommodates several widely used loss functions for the model parameters, including convex, weakly convex, and difference-of-convex loss, and weakly convex sparsity functions to control the complexity of the sample weights. To solve the resulting bivariate problem, we propose an alternating minimization method in which the subproblems for updating the model parameters and weights are each approximated using majorize-minimize techniques. We provide several approximation methods for the loss functions considered in this paper, and show the overall algorithm's convergence. Numerical experiments on various learning tasks and data anomaly settings demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in minimizing the impact of undesirable data points compared to benchmark methods.

items.title: Continual Learning Exam: Benchmarking Long-Horizon RSI and Experiential Learning in LLM Agents
items.summary: Continual learning is the ability of LLM agents to improve over time by acquiring, refining, and applying knowledge from experience while retaining useful prior knowledge. It is essential for agents learning over long time horizons, yet current evaluations largely assess individual task performance rather than improvement through accumulated experience. We introduce Continual Learning Exam (CLE), a large-scale benchmark developed by 50+ domain experts to measure experience-driven improvement in realistic professional workflows. CLE comprises 120 human-authored tasks, each organised as a five-level ladder, yielding 600 levels spanning 89 professional roles across 12 occupational domains. Agents must pass each level to unlock the next, with later levels building on experience accumulated during earlier assignments. An evaluation agent assesses each submission against human-authored rubrics. We compare a single-submission setting with one that provides diagnostic feedback after failure and allows one revision. Across 17 harness-model configurations using frontier LLMs, feedback and revision yield a median completion gain of 5.3 percentage points. Yet the best-performing system clears only 47.7% of levels and completes all five levels in just 23.3% of tasks, highlighting the difficulty of sustained learning from experience for existing frontier LLMs. As such, the dataset can also be used to post-train LLMs to strengthen their continual learning capabilities.

items.title: What Makes a Question Curious? Measuring Model Curiosity in Human-LLM Interactions
items.summary: Large language models increasingly act as partners in everyday communication. In these interactions, useful assistance may require not only answering, but also asking the right questions that surface knowledge gaps, assumptions, and alternatives. In this study, we refer to such epistemic question-asking as model curiosity, and introduce a theory-grounded taxonomy that distinguishes curiosity-oriented questions from generic model questioning. Across four conversation datasets, we find that curiosity-oriented questions remain rare (17-28% of all questions), but are associated with more exploratory and epistemically rich subsequent user responses, with varying patterns across datasets. We further conduct a human study to evaluate the usefulness of model curiosity, finding that curiosity can encourage exploration, especially in advice, creative, and research contexts. These findings have implications for building LLMs that ask more selectively to support deeper exploration and human-AI collaboration.

items.title: Why Does Structured Output Fail? An Empirical Study of Prompt-Enforced Pydantic Schemas Across Nine LLMs
items.summary: Pipelines that require structured outputs from hosted language models often specify a Pydantic schema in the prompt, validate the response, and retry when validation fails. Although native structured-output modes provide an alternative, application-side validation remains important for enforcing custom constraints. Yet pipeline reliability is often summarized by a single validity rate, which obscures why outputs fail and which interventions may help. We introduce a fine-grained taxonomy of schema-conformance failures and a deterministic classifier that assigns failure categories from model responses and Pydantic validation errors. We apply this framework to 3,997 generation attempts across nine OpenAI and Anthropic model/API configurations, using questions from HotpotQA and FinanceBench. Our results show that similar validity rates can mask different failure patterns, and that dominant failure categories vary with schema constraints and task. Markdown-fenced JSON is the most common failure: among 681 fenced failures, only 48.0% pass validation after fence removal, while the remainder conceal additional violations, predominantly field-length violations. In an exploratory prompt ablation, variants that suppress fences appear to shift failures toward length violations, but the shift is consistent with exposing violations that were already present, illustrating how aggregate validity rates can obscure changes in failure composition. We derive four engineering practices for validator, schema, retry and evaluation design, three supported by our data and one, on retry feedback, proposed but not tested, and release the classifier, completions, and annotations.

items.title: Learning Functional Specialisation for Bimanual Robotic Control
items.summary: Bimanual robotic control requires simultaneous management of distinct functional demands under motor noise, energetic costs, and communication delays. We investigate how learning responsibility should be organised across modular controllers and the two arms in a simulated musculoskeletal system with two communicating recurrent controllers. Using a 2 x 2 design, we compare differential versus shared controller objectives and fixed versus balanced hand-task assignments. Task-aligned functional specialisation was strongest when differential objectives were combined with a fixed assignment aligned with contralateral control routing. This condition achieved the highest canonical-task performance and control efficiency, reaching 81.33% bimanual success. Its advantage over shared objectives increased with motor noise but narrowed under stronger energy penalties. Stronger specialisation also reduced hand-role flexibility: reversing the hand roles decreased bimanual success by 80.46 percentage points under Differential-Fixed training, compared with 1.51 percentage points under Shared-Balanced training. These results show that controller objectives and hand-task experience jointly determine functional organisation. Stronger role-specific specialisation favours performance and efficiency when roles remain stable, whereas more distributed training favours interchangeability when roles change.

items.title: Schema-Free Text-to-SQL: Learning Enterprise Database Structure from Query Logs
items.summary: Text-to-SQL systems achieve remarkable accuracy on academic benchmarks, yet performance drops dramatically in enterprise deployments. This gap stems from a fundamental assumption: existing approaches require complete schema documentation, but enterprise databases typically lack comprehensive documentation, featuring cryptic naming and implicit relationships. We present the first text-to-SQL framework that operates without schema documentation, instead learning database structure from historical query logs. Query logs encode implicit structural knowledge: which tables are queried together, how they join, and what columns map to business concepts. We construct a knowledge graph from parsed query patterns and introduce entity-driven GraphRAG retrieval that grounds user questions in domain terminology rather than relying solely on embedding similarity. Validated on both an industrial deployment with expert evaluation and the Beaver benchmark, our approach substantially outperforms similarity-based retrieval methods, the dominant industry approach, in both executability and answer quality. On Beaver, we achieve 95.7% execution validity compared to 60.8% for embedding-based retrieval, with expert data engineers preferring our system 70% to 10% on internal deployment. Our work demonstrates that text-to-SQL can operate effectively in schema-ambiguous enterprise environments, enabling natural language database interfaces "in the wild".

items.title: TurboWAM: Learning What Matters for Fast World Action Models
items.summary: World action models have demonstrated promising performance in robot policy learning, yet their high inference latency remains a critical bottleneck for real-world deployment. Recent approaches have sought to improve inference efficiency by reducing test-time future-frame imagination or accelerating action prediction. However, these methods often leverage representations from all video world model layers without explicitly considering their varying relevance to action prediction, leading to redundant computation and suboptimal representation utilization. In this work, we propose TurboWAM, a fast world action model that efficiently aggregates structured world representations conditioned on action predictions. Specifically, TurboWAM introduces a structured world representation aggregation module that adaptively fuses representations from different world model layers according to their relevance to the evolving action denoising state. Furthermore, TurboWAM employs a structured action supervision mechanism that adaptively modulates gradients from action supervision across different world model layers during backward propagation, facilitating world representation learning. During inference, by reducing the number of world model layers executed and caching relevant representations across action denoising steps, TurboWAM substantially reduces computational overhead. Extensive experiments on multiple robot manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that TurboWAM achieves low inference latency while maintaining competitive task success rates compared with state-of-the-art methods.

items.title: Stable and Calibrated Latent Force ODE Filters
items.summary: Estimating unobserved forces in mechanistic systems is a central task of scientific machine learning. Approximate Gaussian filtering methods that synthesize mechanistic and empirical information have shown remarkable capacity in jointly identifying latent processes together with the system state in a single forward-backward pass. The resulting latent force ODE filter framework channels information from observational data specifically into the unknown parts of the system. This work addresses open questions about calibration and stability of the method. We show that the joint posterior over state and force is the reweighted conventional latent force posterior. This uncovers a crucial dependence of the stability of the method on the prior variance of the system state, which effectively controls the flow of information from observations to the latent force through the mechanistic system. From this insight, we construct an improved algorithm that provides stable and calibrated plug-and-play inference. We demonstrate the improved framework on several simulated experimental settings.

items.title: HerHealthGPT: An Evidence-Grounded Conversational AI System for Women's Reproductive Health Copy title
items.summary: "Why is my period late?" Sometimes, the most useful response begins with another question. Yet conversational AI systems may respond to incomplete health queries without seeking essential context or grounding their guidance in verifiable evidence. This paper introduces HerHealthGPT, an evidence-grounded conversational AI system designed to address these challenges in women's reproductive health. HerHealthGPT integrates retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), context-aware clarification, and source validation within an interactive web interface. Rather than responding immediately to incomplete queries, the system maintains conversational context, asks targeted follow-up questions, checks for premature conclusions, and grounds its responses in retrieved evidence. We evaluate the AI components using 540 English messages derived from 90 reproductive-health cases and conduct a prototype questionnaire study with 30 adults. Evidence retrieval improves concern-category accuracy from 54.1% to 59.3% compared with fine-tuning alone. The clarification router achieves 85.6% recall and 86.2% specificity on constructed targets. In the user study, 83.3% of participants preferred the retrieval-enabled configuration, while 25 of 30 considered its follow-up questions relevant. These findings suggest that integrating evidence retrieval with interactive clarification offers a promising approach to more transparent, context-aware reproductive-health information systems, while further clinical validation remains necessary.

items.title: EnerGNN: Learning Optimization-Compatible Energy Functions for Exact Constrained Combinatorial Inference
items.summary: Learning-based approaches to combinatorial optimization often predict solutions directly or use predictions to restrict search, while expressive energy-based models typically rely on approximate inference. We introduce EnerGNN, a framework that learns energy functions over complete binary configurations and minimizes them under explicit hard constraints through mixed integer programming (MIP). EnerGNN combines a graph neural network encoder with an optimization-compatible readout and a nonlinear energy head, enabling exact constrained inference over the learned energy. An optimality-aware contrastive loss trains the energy to reflect solution quality and constraint violations. Across Quadratic Knapsack, Combinatorial Auctions, and a personalized cell therapy supply chain problem, EnerGNN achieves near-optimal solutions with 100% feasibility. On the supply chain problem, it achieves a 0.05% mean primal gap and a 17.4$\times$ speedup over the monolithic MIP. The learned energy also generalizes to larger instances and supports zero-shot constraint injection, adapting to changing constraints without retraining while preserving feasibility.

items.title: WebViSE: Scaling Visual Design Intelligence from the Open Web for LLM Website Generation
items.summary: Large language models have made remarkable strides in website development, enabling complete and interactive web experiences to be built from natural-language instructions with far less effort. Yet, non-expert users often struggle to articulate sophisticated visual and interaction designs in natural language. Meanwhile, the open web already contains a vast reservoir of such design knowledge, embodied in mature website implementations. To this end, we introduce Website-derived Visual Skill Extraction (WebViSE), a framework that automatically abstracts these implementations into reusable Visual Skills and builds a structured Skill library. To scale the library, WebViSE organizes its Skills in a multi-parent DAG and jointly evolves Skill descriptions and DAG structure using Skill-conditioned Potential Queries, enabling efficient matching between diverse user instructions and relevant Skills. The auto-evolved structure outperforms non-hierarchical LLM retrieval baselines at only 39.09% of the estimated retrieval cost with Qwen3.8-Max. For any models, WebViSE can be directly injected as plug-and-play guidance, enabling diverse models to produce more visually compelling and aesthetically refined web pages. For open-source models, WebViSE can be used to build a data-synthesis pipeline that internalizes visual design intelligence into model weights. Experiments across multiple web development benchmarks and human evaluation consistently show that WebViSE improves the visual quality and interaction fidelity of artifacts. Overall, our work establishes an automated path for extracting, organizing, and transferring design intelligence from the open web to website-building models. We release all extracted Visual Skills, the associated Skill DAG, and our code at https://github.com/YifeiSun-0710/WebViSE.

items.title: Multitask Interactions in Recurrent Dynamics across 100 Cognitive Tasks
items.summary: The brain continually learns tasks with very different computational demands. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have been used as dynamical surrogates for studying task solutions, with recent work extending this approach to joint training on multitask batteries. However, it remains unclear how tasks interact as these batteries grow in scale and heterogeneity: under what conditions do they transfer or interfere with one another, and how do these effects relate to task complexity and model structure? We study this question by simultaneously training hierarchical Almost-Linear RNNs (AL-RNNs) on 100 tasks spanning a wide range of cognitive demands. AL-RNNs allow us to vary the amount of nonlinearity in the recurrence, while hierarchical task features provide a low-dimensional interface for task-specific adaptation within shared dynamics. On this task battery, performance improves with both nonlinear capacity and task-feature dimensionality, with the joint hierarchical model outperforming both individually trained models and a single unstructured joint model. Many tasks are individually solvable with linear dynamics, yet cannot be solved together by a shared linear model. Through hierarchical task features, task-specific linear region usage, and task geometry, the trained model provides several related but distinct measures of task similarity that capture how computations are separated and combined within the shared backbone. Across a series of experiments, we relate these representations to individual task complexity, joint solvability, pairwise transfer learning, and leave-one-out adaptation. Together, our experiments characterize task interactions in multitask recurrent learning while demonstrating both the potential and the challenges of reusable dynamical backbones for cognitive computation.

items.title: Neural Eigenfluid Bases: Spectral Objectives, Gauge, and Topology
items.summary: Reduced-order models simplify fluid simulation by representing complex flows with a small number of spatial modes. Building on Laplacian Eigenfluids, we introduce Neural Eigenfluid Bases (NEB), a neural representation whose basis functions can be evaluated anywhere in space. We enforce incompressibility and impermeable boundaries directly through differential lifts and potential boundary conditions. Geometry-local orthogonalization and Rayleigh minimization then learn an ordered basis. We connect learning in potential and velocity spaces, and derive a spectral-variance relation explaining why these objectives weight approximate modes differently, even though their exact positive spectra agree. Gauge fixing reduces the number of spatial derivatives needed for potential learning, while a Dirichlet energy loss learns independent circulation fields around obstacles. With 1024 modes, both objectives keep velocity errors below 1% in periodic vortex merger. For random flows around obstacles, potential-based learning captures more initial energy and gives lower final errors than numerical Laplacian bases of the same size. The reduced state is about a thousand times smaller than the full reference model. Three-dimensional tests separate spatial reconstruction errors from errors in coefficient evolution. Precomputed Galerkin operators allow millisecond-scale updates when the same basis is reused across simulations. This provides a physically constrained basis for continuous flow reconstruction and efficient reduced-order simulation.

items.title: Learning Population Dynamics with Variational Doob-Wasserstein Flow
items.summary: This paper introduces a novel simulation-free framework for learning unbalanced population dynamics on the Riemannian Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao (WFR) manifold, termed Variational Doob-Wasserstein Flow (VDWF), built upon the theory of the unbalanced mean-field Schrödinger bridge (MFSB). First, by independently learning a geometry model equipped with a data-dependent metric, our model captures the intrinsic geometric structure of population dynamics. Furthermore, leveraging Doob's h-transform, the proposed method incorporates boundary information to improve flow-based trajectory inference. For unbalanced transport, a growth model is employed to learn the dynamics while constructing intermediate mass samples in the WFR space without simulation. Additionally, we analyze the convergence rate of the proposed framework using a uniform Log-Sobolev inequality (LSI). Finally, we validate the proposed approach on multiple real-world datasets, demonstrating competitive performance in learning both balanced and unbalanced population dynamics compared with state-of-the-art methods.

items.title: Real-Time Human Trajectory Prediction from RGB-D for Mobile Robots Using Bi-Mamba
items.summary: Predicting the short-term future trajectory of a person from RGB-D cameras is a key capability for mobile robots navigating in dynamic and human populated environment. The key challenge to deploying learned predictors on real robots is the train-deploy pipeline gap. Training data are often prepared with an idealized, smoothed ground truth, whereas at inference, the model is fed noisy estimates from pose detectors and depth sensors. The model is therefore evaluated on an input distribution it never encountered during training. Most existing models rely on recurrent neural networks (RNNs) or transformers, which either struggle to capture short-term temporal dependencies or suffer from computational cost. We present TrajMamba, a lightweight, bidirectional state space model for short-term human trajectory prediction using an RGB-D camera. The model uses a single shared processing path for both training and deployment, aligning human pose extraction, depth back projection, and smoothing processes. It encodes a short window of persons's hip center velocities with stacked bidirectional Mamba blocks and decodes future velocities with a GRU head. On the ETH/UCY benchmark, TrajMamba reaches an average ADE of 0.29 m FDE of 0.51 m. With 262K parameters, it runs in real time on modest hardware and is deployed on a TIAGo robot with an onboard NVIDIA Jetson Orin.

items.title: Texture-Aware Strategies for Subregion Style Transfer Augmentation
items.summary: A common strategy for data augmentation is to apply style transfer on training images to enrich appearance variations. Recent approaches have combined style augmentation with random erasing by selectively replacing image subregions with style-transferred patches. However, existing methods rely on uniformly random region selection or fixed geometric constraints, which may fail to cover informative texture patterns and limit augmentation diversity. To address these limitations, we propose a texture-aware subregion style augmentation framework that prioritizes regions with strong texture responses for style replacement. Furthermore, we extend this framework with a hybrid region strategy that combines a texture-driven region with an auxiliary random region, implicitly enabling more diverse style perturbations. Experiments demonstrate that our approach achieves higher classification accuracy and improves robustness compared with existing style-based augmentation methods.

items.title: Rank-1 Weight-Corrected Trainable Weight Averaging for Out-of-Distribution Detection
items.summary: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection identifies inputs outside the training distribution. Rank-based analyses such as RankFeat and RankWeight suggest that OOD overconfidence is closely related to dominant low-rank components in feature and weight spaces. Since weight averaging operates directly in parameter space and improves model generalization, we consider it for OOD detection from a dominant-component perspective. Trainable Weight Averaging (TWA) assigns a single coefficient to each checkpoint, limiting independent control of dominant weight components. We extend TWA with leading rank-one weight components extracted by Singular Value Decomposition as correction directions, whose contributions are learned through the in-distribution classification objective. On ResNet50, our method improves over fine-tuning and standard TWA across the evaluated datasets with MSP and RankWeight, both with and without Outlier Exposure. Mahalanobis-based evaluation yields mixed results, indicating that the benefit depends on the OOD scoring protocol. Target-layer analyses with MSP and Energy favor correction near the classifier.

items.title: OS-Wizard: Scaling Computer-Using Agents to Specialized Software via Knowledge-Guided Exploration
items.summary: Computer-using agents are increasingly capable of performing complex tasks in the digital world. However, high-quality interaction trajectories remain scarce for specialized desktop applications, where limited application knowledge, cumbersome GUI workflows, and incomplete exploration hinder automated collection. We introduce OS-Wizard, an automated trajectory collection framework. It combines tutorial-guided exploration with a hybrid GUI--Code action space, providing application-specific knowledge and simplifying GUI workflows through direct execution of application-native commands. The framework also checkpoints and revisits pivotal states during tree exploration to explore alternative workflows, complementing linear rollouts for broader coverage. We collect 10.9K trajectories comprising 54.9K state--action samples. Fine-tuning open-source base models on this corpus yields a best-performing model that improves performance on a benchmark of specialized desktop workflows by 58.2 percentage points to 64.1\%, surpassing reported human performance of 59.8\% and establishing a new state of the art. The fine-tuned model also improves performance on general desktop workflows using GUI actions only, suggesting that the collected supervision benefits general desktop tasks as well. Comparative experiments and ablations demonstrate the efficiency of trajectory collection and the importance of code actions.

items.title: Sybil-Resilient Multi-Drone Exploration of Indoor and Confined Spaces
items.summary: When a team of drones explores a building together, each drone tells the others which frontier it is going to and shares the map it has built. This avoids duplicated effort, but it also means that the team trusts every identity from which it receives messages. In a Sybil attack, one compromised drone creates fake identities, and these fake teammates claim frontiers and send fabricated scans, so the real drones leave parts of the building unexplored and end up with walls in their maps that do not exist. We study five such attackers, including one that seals off the openings between floors, and five levels of defence that need no security infrastructure, only the drones' own sensors and maps: an audit of received map data against what a drone sees itself, a check that a body is present where an identity claims to be, trust only for identities whose body has been seen, a quarantine for identities that no drone has observed, and a rule that binds each observed body to one identity. Tests in simulation cover 70 maps of seven kinds, from offices and tunnels to three-storey buildings and caves. Without a defence, one compromised drone leaves on average up to 25% of a map unexplored (45% in offices), and the floor-sealing attacker cuts the explored part of a three-storey building to 82.3%, or 34.6% on the worst map. The quarantine brings exploration back to the level of an unattacked team in every setting, and in most settings it also brings the false data back to that level. The exceptions are two colluding attackers, fakes placed next to real drones, three of the ten caves and a team of 16 drones, and binding bodies to identities fixes the last three. Over 2,350 missions, an honest drone was revoked by a teammate only twice.
